system:
You are shown a snapshot of US macroeconomic and market data as it was known at the end of one month between 2007 and 2026.

Estimate which month the snapshot describes. Use only the figures supplied plus your general knowledge of economic history.

Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"year": yyyy, "month": m, "confidence": c, "cues": ["...", "..."]}
Rules: year is an integer from 2007 to 2026; month is an integer from 1 to 12; c in [0, 1] is your confidence that the guess is within 6 months of the truth; 1 to 3 short cues citing the inputs.
text:
This looks like a period with a strong dollar, a very low unemployment rate relative to the last 36 months, a flat or inverted yield curve, and core CPI high. The policy rate has risen over 3 months (+1.0), and the 10-year yield is low relative to its 3-year range. Gold is weak.

The candidates are mid-2018, 2019, 2023, and 2024-25. The 3-year window for the policy rate is only +0.5, with a +1.0 3-month change, so the Fed is hiking, and the 10-year yield is low (-2.0) while the 2-year is -1.0. The spread is very negative (-2.5) and unemployment is low (-2.0). That fits late 2018, when the Fed was hiking. But the 10-year yield z of -2.0 doesn't fit 2018, when yields were rising. The dollar is +2.0, which fits 2015 or 2018, but those years are within the data range only partly.

Consider late 2000s instead: the data starts in 2007, but the z-scores need 36 months of history.

Another candidate is 2022-23. In 2022 the policy rate z would be much higher than +0.5, so that doesn't fit.

Consider early 2020: the policy rate z would be low then, so no.

Consider the first half of 2019: the 10-year yield was falling, the VIX was higher and credit spreads were wider, but gold was not weak, so no.

Consider late 2018 (Dec): the VIX was +1.0 over 3 months, credit spreads were wider and equities were weak, but the 12-month equity change was only -0.5. Gold was weak in 2018 (down to August), and the dollar was strong, but the 10-year yield z of -2.0 doesn't fit.

Consider 2025-26: the policy rate z of +0.5 with a +1.0 3-month change doesn't fit cuts.

Consider the 2023 summer: the policy rate z would be very high, so no.

Consider 2007 itself: the data may use a shorter history. Core CPI +1.5 and unemployment -2.0 could fit 2007, but the dollar was weak then and gold was strong, so no.

Consider 2015-16: the dollar was strong (+2.0), gold was weak (-2.5 at 6 months), the 10-year yield was low (-2.0 vs. the 2012-15 history of higher yields), the policy rate had just risen (Dec 2015: +1.0 3-month change from 0.25 to 0.5), and unemployment was low at 5.0%. The VIX was up, credit spreads were wider (energy), and equities were weak. Core CPI was +1.5, which is plausible. Treasuries were up 1m. The best match is Jan-Feb 2016; the 10-year yield fell in January 2016, and 1-month 20y+ returns were +2.0, which fits. Equities were -1.5 for the month, which fits January 2016 (the S&P fell about 5%, which would be larger), so perhaps December 2015 (S&P -1.6%, Treasuries slightly up). However, the 1m Treasury return of +1.5 favors January 2016, and the 3m equity at -1.0 fits too. I'll go with January 2016.
